questions.q: Which specialized intercellular structures at intercalated discs provide low-resistance electrical coupling so that cardiac myocytes function as a functional syncytium?
options: Gap junctions (nexuses)
Tight junctions (zonula occludens)
Hemidesmosomes
Myelin sheaths
questions.explain: Intercalated discs contain fasciae adherentes and desmosomes for mechanical anchoring plus gap junctions (connexons) that allow ions to pass rapidly from cell to cell, coordinating synchronous atrial and ventricular contraction.

open.q: Name the low-resistance channels within intercalated discs that electrically couple adjacent cardiac muscle fibers into a functional syncytium.
accept: Gap junctions
Nexus
Connexons

questions.q: Why does an action potential originating in the atria normally reach the ventricles exclusively through the atrioventricular (AV) bundle rather than spreading directly across the myocardial wall?
options: Atrial myocytes lack gap junctions
The fibrous skeleton electrically insulates atria from ventricles
The epicardium absorbs impulses at the coronary sulcus
Ventricular cells remain refractory to atrial impulses
questions.explain: Dense fibrous rings surrounding the heart valves separate the atrial and ventricular muscle masses electrically, forcing impulses through the AV node and bundle of His so atria finish contracting before ventricles eject.

open.q: What anatomical structure electrically insulates the atrial syncytium from the ventricular syncytium but NOT at the AV bundle?
accept: Fibrous skeleton of the heart
Cardiac fibrous skeleton
Annuli fibrosi

questions.q: How does excitation-contraction coupling in ventricular cardiac muscle differ critically from that in skeletal muscle?
options: Cardiac muscle lacks troponin C and uses calmodulin
Cardiac contraction needs no extracellular calcium
L-type Ca2+ entry triggers RyR2-mediated calcium-induced calcium release
Cardiac T-tubules lie at the A–I junction
questions.explain: In cardiac myocytes, plateau Ca2+ entry via dihydropyridine L-type Ca2+ channels binds ryanodine receptor 2 (RyR2) on the sarcoplasmic reticulum to trigger massive Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release; in skeletal muscle, DHPR mechanically opens RyR1 without needing extracellular Ca2+ influx.

open.q: Explain why cardiac muscle contraction fails in a calcium-free extracellular solution whereas skeletal muscle can still contract.
accept: Cardiac muscle requires extracellular Ca2+ influx through L-type channels to trigger calcium-induced calcium release
Calcium-induced calcium release depends on extracellular Ca2+ entry

questions.q: Which ionic current is responsible for the rapid Phase 0 depolarization upstroke in normal ventricular and atrial working myocytes?
options: Slow inward Ca2+ current through T-type channels
Outward K+ current through Ik1 inward rectifier channels
Inward Na+ current through hyperpolarization-activated HCN funny channels
Rapid inward Na+ current through voltage-gated fast Na+ channels
questions.explain: When ventricular myocytes depolarize from -90 mV to threshold (-70 mV), fast voltage-gated Na+ channels open explosively, driving membrane potential toward +20 mV during Phase 0.

open.q: Which ion channel mediates the rapid Phase 0 upstroke of the ventricular cardiac muscle action potential?
accept: Fast voltage-gated sodium channels
Voltage-gated Na+ channels
Fast Na+ channels

questions.q: Which balance of transmembrane ion currents maintains the prolonged Phase 2 plateau of the ventricular cardiac action potential?
options: L-type Ca2+ influx is balanced by delayed-rectifier K+ efflux
Cl− influx is balanced by Na+/K+-ATPase
Funny-channel Na+ influx is balanced by Ca2+ extrusion
All sarcolemmal channels close
questions.explain: During Phase 2 (~150-200 ms), sustained Ca2+ influx via L-type channels offsets outward K+ current (IKr/IKs), prolonging depolarization and the effective refractory period so cardiac muscle cannot undergo tetanic summation.

open.q: Which two opposing ionic currents balance each other to produce the Phase 2 plateau of the ventricular action potential?
accept: Inward Ca2+ current (L-type) and outward K+ current (delayed rectifier)
Calcium influx and potassium efflux

questions.q: Why is cardiac muscle physiologically incapable of undergoing sustained tetanic contraction like skeletal muscle?
options: Cardiac muscle lacks myosin ATPase
The prolonged phase-2 plateau extends the absolute refractory period through most of the twitch
Cardiac SR contains no calcium
Vagal activity continuously blocks ventricular cross-bridges
questions.explain: Because fast Na+ channels remain inactivated throughout the prolonged plateau (~200-250 ms), the cardiac absolute refractory period lasts nearly as long as the mechanical twitch, ensuring adequate ventricular filling between beats. Key detail: The phase-2 plateau prolongs refractoriness until near the end of contraction.

open.q: What electrophysiological property prevents cardiac muscle from being tetanized?
accept: Long absolute refractory period caused by the action potential plateau
Prolonged refractory period matching the duration of mechanical contraction

questions.q: Which ionic mechanism underlies the spontaneous Phase 4 pacemaker prepotential in sinoatrial (SA) nodal cells?
options: Fast Na+ channels open at −90 mV
Muscarinic K+ channels increase outward current
HCN funny current and T-type Ca2+ entry depolarise the pacemaker cell
Na+/K+/2Cl− cotransport is activated
questions.explain: SA nodal cells lack a stable resting membrane potential (~-60 mV maximum diastolic potential); repolarization opens hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated (HCN) 'funny' channels admitting Na+, aided by T-type Ca2+ channels and K+ channel closure until threshold (-40 mV) triggers an L-type Ca2+ upstroke.

open.q: Name the primary pacemaker current responsible for spontaneous Phase 4 diastolic depolarization in the sinoatrial node.
accept: Funny current (If)
HCN channel Na+ current
Inward Na+ funny current

questions.q: Which ion channel mediates the Phase 0 depolarization upstroke in SA node and AV node pacemaker action potentials?
options: Fast voltage-gated Na+ channels
Inward rectifier K+ channels
Chloride leak channels
Slow L-type voltage-gated Ca2+ channels
questions.explain: Because SA and AV nodal cells have a less negative maximum diastolic potential (~-60 mV), fast Na+ channels remain inactivated; Phase 0 is driven by slower L-type Ca2+ influx, explaining slow AV nodal conduction velocity.

open.q: Which ion channels generate the Phase 0 upstroke in sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodal cells?
accept: L-type calcium channels
Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels
Slow Ca2+ channels

questions.q: Which sequence accurately traces normal cardiac impulse conduction from initiation to ventricular activation?
options: SA node → AV node → His bundle → bundle branches → Purkinje fibres
AV node → SA node → Purkinje fibres → His bundle
SA node → His bundle → AV node → Purkinje fibres
Purkinje fibres → AV node → SA node
questions.explain: Impulses originate in the SA node (~70-80 bpm), cross the atria via anterior, middle, and posterior internodal tracts, pause ~0.1 s at the AV node, and descend rapidly through the His-Purkinje system.

open.q: List the anatomical pathway of electrical impulse conduction through the heart starting at the sinoatrial node.
accept: SA node, internodal pathways, AV node, bundle of His, bundle branches, Purkinje fibers
SA node -> AV node -> bundle of His -> bundle branches -> Purkinje fibers

questions.q: What is the physiological purpose of the ~0.1-second conduction delay at the atrioventricular (AV) node?
options: To slow ventricular ejection
To permit atrial contraction and ventricular filling before systole
To prevent coronary venous reflux
To synchronise semilunar valve closure
questions.explain: Small fiber diameter, fewer gap junctions, and Ca2+-dependent depolarization slow conduction through the AV node (~0.05 m/s), ensuring atrial systole tops off ventricular end-diastolic volume prior to ventricular contraction.

open.q: Why is the physiological conduction delay at the atrioventricular (AV) node essential for cardiac pumping efficiency?
accept: Allows atrial contraction to complete ventricular filling before ventricular contraction begins
Gives atria time to empty blood into the ventricles prior to ventricular systole

questions.q: Which component of the cardiac conduction system exhibits the fastest conduction velocity (~4 m/s) to ensure near-simultaneous depolarization of both ventricles?
options: AV nodal transitional zone
Atrial working myocardium
Purkinje fibers
SA nodal pacemaker center
questions.explain: Purkinje fibers have large diameters and dense connexin-40 gap junctions, conducting impulses at 1.5 to 4.0 m/s so ventricular contraction proceeds smoothly from apex toward base.

open.q: Name the cardiac conduction tissue with the highest conduction velocity (~4 m/s).
accept: Purkinje system
Subendocardial Purkinje network

questions.q: Why does the sinoatrial (SA) node normally serve as the dominant pacemaker of the heart rather than the AV node or Purkinje fibers?
options: Only the SA node receives sympathetic fibres
AV node and Purkinje fibres lack HCN channels
The SA node is nearest the left ventricle
The SA node has the steepest phase-4 depolarisation and fastest intrinsic rate
questions.explain: SA nodal cells reach threshold fastest (intrinsic ~100/min, resting ~70/min under vagal tone), depolarizing the AV node (intrinsic 40-60/min) and Purkinje fibers (15-40/min) before they can spontaneously fire (overdrive suppression). Key detail: The SA node has the steepest phase-4 depolarisation and fastest intrinsic rate.

open.q: Why does the sinoatrial node normally dominate over latent pacemakers in the AV node and Purkinje system?
accept: It has the fastest intrinsic depolarization rate and suppresses slower pacemakers via overdrive suppression
Fastest spontaneous Phase 4 depolarization rate

questions.q: At a normal resting heart rate of 75 beats per minute, what is the total duration of one cardiac cycle and its approximate division between ventricular systole and diastole?
options: 0.80 seconds total: 0.30 seconds systole and 0.50 seconds diastole
1.00 second total: 0.50 seconds systole and 0.50 seconds diastole
0.60 seconds total: 0.40 seconds systole and 0.20 seconds diastole
1.20 seconds total: 0.80 seconds systole and 0.40 seconds diastole
questions.explain: At 75 bpm, cycle length = 60 / 75 = 0.80 s, comprising ~0.30 s of ventricular systole and ~0.50 s of ventricular diastole; when heart rate increases markedly, diastole shortens disproportionately more than systole.

open.q: At a heart rate of 75 beats/min, state the total duration of a cardiac cycle and the respective durations of ventricular systole and diastole.
accept: 0.8 s total; 0.3 s systole and 0.5 s diastole
0.80 seconds (0.30 s systole, 0.50 s diastole)

questions.q: What is the status of the atrioventricular (mitral/tricuspid) and semilunar (aortic/pulmonary) valves during isovolumetric ventricular contraction?
options: AV valves open and semilunar valves closed
Both AV valves and semilunar valves closed
AV valves closed and semilunar valves open
Both AV valves and semilunar valves open
questions.explain: Isovolumetric contraction begins immediately after AV valve closure (S1) while ventricular pressure rises steeply from ~8 mmHg to ~80 mmHg (left ventricle), before exceeding aortic diastolic pressure to open the semilunar valves; volume remains constant at EDV.

open.q: Are the atrioventricular and semilunar valves open or closed during isovolumetric ventricular contraction?
accept: All four valves are closed
Both AV and semilunar valves are closed

questions.q: What event initiates the phase of rapid ventricular ejection during systole?
options: Mitral and tricuspid valve closure
Atrial systole
LV pressure exceeds aortic diastolic pressure, opening the aortic valve
Ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure
questions.explain: Once left ventricular pressure surpasses ~80 mmHg (and right ventricular pressure surpasses ~8-10 mmHg), the semilunar valves open and ~70% of stroke volume is ejected rapidly during the first third of ejection.

open.q: What pressure event terminates isovolumetric contraction and initiates ventricular ejection?
accept: Ventricular pressure exceeds aortic (and pulmonary) diastolic pressure, opening the semilunar valves
Left ventricular pressure rises above aortic pressure (~80 mmHg)

questions.q: Which sequence of valve events defines the boundaries of isovolumetric ventricular relaxation?
options: Begins with mitral valve closure and ends with aortic valve opening
Begins with aortic valve opening and ends with mitral valve closure
Begins with atrial contraction and ends with tricuspid valve closure
Begins with aortic/pulmonary valve closure (S2) and ends with mitral/tricuspid valve opening
questions.explain: When ventricular pressure falls below aortic/pulmonary pressure at the end of systole, semilunar valves snap shut (S2); ventricular pressure then plummets rapidly with all valves closed at End-Systolic Volume until falling below atrial pressure to open the AV valves.

open.q: Which valve events mark the start and the end of isovolumetric ventricular relaxation?
accept: Starts with semilunar valve closure and ends with AV valve opening
Aortic/pulmonary valve closure to mitral/tricuspid valve opening

questions.q: In a healthy young adult at rest, roughly what percentage of ventricular filling occurs passively before atrial contraction (atrial kick) takes place?
questions.explain: About 75-80% of blood flows passively from atria to ventricles during rapid filling and diastasis; atrial systole contributes the final 20-25% ('atrial kick'), which becomes crucial during tachycardia or ventricular hypertrophy.

open.q: Approximately what percentage of ventricular filling is contributed by atrial systole ('atrial kick') versus passive filling at rest?
accept: 20% to 25% by atrial systole and 75% to 80% passive
About 20% atrial contraction, 80% passive

questions.q: In a healthy resting adult with an end-diastolic volume (EDV) of 120 mL and an end-systolic volume (ESV) of 50 mL, what are the stroke volume (SV) and ejection fraction (EF)?
options: SV = 170 mL and EF = 42%
SV = 70 mL and EF = 58.3%
SV = 50 mL and EF = 70%
SV = 70 mL and EF = 35%
questions.explain: Stroke Volume = EDV - ESV = 120 - 50 = 70 mL. Ejection Fraction = (SV / EDV) x 100 = (70 / 120) x 100 = 58.3% (normal resting EF is 55% to 70%).

open.q: Calculate stroke volume and ejection fraction if end-diastolic volume is 120 mL and end-systolic volume is 50 mL.
accept: Stroke volume 70 mL and ejection fraction 58.3%
SV = 70 mL, EF = 58%

questions.sub: Heart Sounds and Jugular Venous Pulse
questions.q: What causes the first heart sound (S1) and the second heart sound (S2), respectively?
options: S1: AV valves open; S2: semilunar valves open
S1: rapid filling; S2: atrial contraction
S1: AV valve closure; S2: semilunar valve closure
S1: aortic closure; S2: mitral closure
questions.explain: Heart sounds arise from sudden deceleration of blood and valve leaflet vibration upon closure: S1 ('lub') marks AV valve closure at the start of isovolumetric contraction, while S2 ('dup') marks semilunar valve closure at the start of isovolumetric relaxation.

open.q: State the valvular events responsible for producing the first (S1) and second (S2) heart sounds.
accept: S1 is closure of AV (mitral and tricuspid) valves; S2 is closure of semilunar (aortic and pulmonary) valves
AV valve closure for S1 and semilunar valve closure for S2

questions.sub: Heart Sounds and Jugular Venous Pulse
questions.q: Why does physiological splitting of the second heart sound (S2) widen during normal inspiration?
options: Inspiration delays A2
Inspiration causes premature P2
Inspiration reduces right atrial return
Inspiration increases RV filling, delaying P2 and slightly advancing A2
questions.explain: Negative intrathoracic pressure during inspiration augments systemic venous return to the right heart (prolonging RV ejection and delaying P2) while pooling blood in pulmonary vessels (reducing LV preload and advancing A2). Key detail: Inspiration increases right ventricular filling, delaying P2 and slightly advancing A2.

open.q: Explain why the A2 and P2 components of the second heart sound separate (split) during inspiration.
accept: Inspiration increases venous return to the right ventricle, delaying pulmonary valve closure (P2), while decreasing left ventricular filling and advancing A2
Delayed P2 from increased right heart filling and earlier A2

questions.sub: Heart Sounds and Jugular Venous Pulse
questions.q: When do the third (S3) and fourth (S4) heart sounds occur during the cardiac cycle, and what does S4 indicate in an adult?
options: S3: early rapid filling; S4: atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle
S3 occurs during isovolumetric contraction; S4 during ejection
S3 occurs during relaxation; S4 after S1
Both occur only during systole
questions.explain: S3 is caused by blood oscillating against ventricular walls during rapid early diastolic filling (normal in children/pregnancy, pathologic in systolic heart failure); S4 ('atrial gallop') is always pathologic in adults, caused by forceful atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle (e.g., concentric LVH or ischemia). Key detail: S3 occurs during rapid filling; S4 occurs when atria contract against a stiff ventricle.

open.q: Identify the phase of the cardiac cycle in which S3 and S4 occur and state what a fourth heart sound (S4) signifies.
accept: S3 occurs in early rapid ventricular filling; S4 occurs in late diastole during atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle
S3: early diastole; S4: late diastole (atrial kick against a non-compliant ventricle)

questions.sub: Heart Sounds and Jugular Venous Pulse
questions.q: In the jugular venous pressure (JVP) tracing, what produces the 'a' wave, the 'c' wave, and the 'v' wave?
options: a: ventricular ejection; c: atrial relaxation; v: tricuspid opening
a: atrial contraction; c: tricuspid bulging; v: atrial filling against a closed valve
a: aortic closure; c: rapid filling; v: atrial systole
a: carotid artefact; c: P2 closure; v: isovolumetric relaxation
questions.explain: The JVP waveform reflects right atrial pressure changes: 'a' = atrial contraction (absent in atrial fibrillation), 'c' = tricuspid bulging in early systole, 'x' descent = atrial relaxation/downward pulling of tricuspid ring, 'v' = venous filling during late systole, and 'y' descent = passive emptying upon tricuspid opening. Key detail: a: atrial contraction; c: tricuspid bulging during isovolumetric contraction; v: venous filling against closed tricuspid valve.

open.q: State the physiological causes of the a, c, and v waves in the jugular venous pulse (JVP) curve.
accept: a: atrial contraction; c: tricuspid valve bulging during isovolumetric contraction; v: atrial venous filling against closed tricuspid valve
a wave = atrial systole, c wave = tricuspid bulging, v wave = venous filling

questions.sub: Heart Sounds and Jugular Venous Pulse
questions.q: What produces the incisura (dicrotic notch) visible on the descending limb of the aortic pressure curve?
options: Mitral valve opening
Atrial contraction
Aortic recoil and brief retrograde flow after aortic valve closure
Peak ventricular ejection
questions.explain: At the end of systole, brief backflow of aortic blood snaps the aortic valve shut, causing a sharp transient pressure dip (incisura/dicrotic notch) followed by a secondary wave from aortic elastic recoil (Windkessel effect).

open.q: What physiological event causes the incisura (dicrotic notch) on the aortic pressure tracing?
accept: Closure of the aortic valve and elastic recoil of the aorta
Sudden closure of the aortic semilunar valve

questions.q: On a left ventricular pressure-volume (PV) loop, what does the width of the loop along the horizontal volume axis represent, and what does the enclosed area of the loop represent?
options: Width: heart rate; area: peripheral resistance
Width: end-systolic pressure; area: oxygen use
Width: ejection fraction; area: vascular compliance
Width: stroke volume; area: external stroke work
questions.explain: The vertical segments represent isovolumetric contraction (right) and isovolumetric relaxation (left) separated horizontally by Stroke Volume (EDV - ESV), while the area inside the loop equals external stroke work (Pressure x Volume).

open.q: In a left ventricular pressure-volume loop, what physiological quantities are represented by the width of the loop and the area inside the loop?
accept: Width = stroke volume; area = stroke work
Horizontal width is stroke volume and enclosed area is external stroke work

questions.q: How does an isolated increase in afterload (such as acute systemic hypertension) alter the left ventricular pressure-volume loop?
options: Higher peak systolic pressure, higher ESV and lower stroke volume
Lower peak pressure, lower ESV and higher stroke volume
Leftward shift of ESPVR
Loss of isovolumetric relaxation
questions.explain: Increased afterload forces the ventricle to generate higher pressure before opening the aortic valve, shortening ejection duration so ESV increases along the unchanged ESPVR line and stroke volume falls.

open.q: Describe how an acute increase in afterload changes peak ventricular systolic pressure, end-systolic volume (ESV), and stroke volume on a pressure-volume loop.
accept: Increases peak systolic pressure and ESV, and decreases stroke volume
Higher ejection pressure, higher ESV, lower SV

questions.q: How does administration of a positive inotropic agent (such as dobutamine or norepinephrine) affect the end-systolic pressure-volume relationship (ESPVR) and end-systolic volume?
options: Lower ESPVR slope and higher ESV
Higher ESPVR slope, lower ESV and higher stroke volume
Higher EDV with unchanged ESV and ESPVR
Lower preload and contractility
questions.explain: Enhanced myocardial contractility increases the slope (Emax) of the ESPVR line, enabling the ventricle to eject more forcefully to a smaller end-systolic volume (ESV) and larger stroke volume.

open.q: How does increased myocardial contractility shift the end-systolic pressure-volume relationship (ESPVR) and affect end-systolic volume?
accept: Shifts ESPVR upward and leftward (steeper slope), decreasing ESV
Increases ESPVR slope and lowers end-systolic volume

questions.q: What does the Frank-Starling law of the heart state?
options: Heart rate always rises with blood pressure
Coronary flow occurs mainly during peak systole
Within limits, increased filling stretches sarcomeres and raises stroke volume
Contractility is independent of intracellular calcium
questions.explain: Greater venous return stretches ventricular myocytes (increasing preload/EDV toward optimal sarcomere length ~2.2 um), increasing troponin C sensitivity to Ca2+ and cross-bridge overlap to augment stroke volume.

open.q: State the Frank-Starling law of the heart.
accept: Force of cardiac contraction and stroke volume increase in proportion to end-diastolic volume (venous return)
Within physiological limits, stroke volume increases as end-diastolic fiber length increases

questions.q: How does sympathetic stimulation via beta-1 adrenergic receptors accelerate myocardial relaxation (positive lusitropy)?
options: Inhibiting sarcolemmal Na+/K+-ATPase
Opening muscarinic K+ channels
Blocking SR ryanodine receptors
PKA phosphorylates phospholamban, relieving SERCA inhibition
questions.explain: Beta-1 Gs-cAMP-PKA signaling phosphorylates L-type Ca2+ channels (increasing Ca2+ entry/inotropy), troponin I (accelerating Ca2+ dissociation), and phospholamban (disinhibiting SERCA2a to speed diastolic Ca2+ reuptake/lusitropy).

open.q: Explain the intracellular mechanism by which beta-1 adrenergic stimulation produces a positive lusitropic (faster relaxation) effect in cardiac myocytes.
accept: PKA phosphorylates phospholamban, stimulating SERCA to rapidly reuptake Ca2+ into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Phosphorylation of phospholamban increases SR Ca2+-ATPase activity

questions.q: By which membrane mechanism does vagal parasympathetic stimulation (acetylcholine acting on M2 muscarinic receptors) slow the heart rate (negative chronotropy)?
options: M2–Gi opens K-ACh channels and lowers cAMP, hyperpolarising SA cells and slowing phase 4
Increasing cAMP accelerates HCN opening
Activating alpha-1 receptors on Purkinje fibres
Opening fast Na+ channels in the AV node
questions.explain: M2 receptors couple to Gi proteins: the beta-gamma subunit directly opens GIRK (K-ACh) channels to hyperpolarize maximum diastolic potential, while alpha-i inhibits adenylyl cyclase, flattening Phase 4 slope. Key detail: Opening K-ACh channels hyperpolarises SA cells and lowers cAMP-dependent currents.

open.q: How does acetylcholine binding to cardiac M2 muscarinic receptors reduce the firing rate of the sinoatrial node?
accept: Opens K-ACh channels to hyperpolarize the membrane and lowers cAMP to slow Phase 4 funny and Ca2+ currents
Hyperpolarizes SA nodal cells via K+ efflux and slows diastolic depolarization

questions.q: A 68-year-old man with long-standing untreated systemic hypertension develops concentric left ventricular hypertrophy and a prominent fourth heart sound (S4) without a murmur. During which phase of the cardiac cycle is S4 generated, and why is it absent if he develops atrial fibrillation?
options: Early rapid ventricular filling; atrial fibrillation speeds ventricular relaxation
Late diastole during atrial systole; atrial fibrillation abolishes organized atrial contraction
Isovolumetric contraction; atrial fibrillation prevents mitral valve closure
Mid-systolic ejection; atrial fibrillation lowers aortic pressure
questions.explain: S4 is produced by forceful atrial contraction pushing blood into a stiff, hypertrophied ventricle at the end of diastole; because atrial fibrillation eliminates coordinated atrial contraction (and the JVP 'a' wave), S4 disappears.

open.q: Why does a fourth heart sound (S4) disappear if a patient with left ventricular hypertrophy develops atrial fibrillation?
accept: Atrial fibrillation eliminates coordinated atrial contraction needed to generate S4
S4 depends on atrial systole, which is lost in atrial fibrillation
